## Purpose

A production HTTP gateway needs separate connection, first-byte, idle-stream, and total-request timeouts because each bounds a different phase or failure pattern. The connection timeout limits establishing an upstream connection, including relevant transport and TLS setup. The first-byte timeout limits waiting for an upstream response after sending the request. The idle-stream timeout limits silence between response reads, allowing legitimately long streams that keep making progress. The total-request timeout caps overall lifetime, including retries and streaming, so incremental progress cannot consume resources indefinitely.

## Failure modes

Without a connection deadline, unreachable upstreams can tie up sockets and pending work. Without a first-byte deadline, an accepted request can wait indefinitely behind a stalled application. Without an idle deadline, a response that starts successfully can hang midway. Without a total deadline, a peer can send occasional bytes forever. One timeout cannot safely replace the others: a short universal limit breaks healthy long-running responses, while a generous limit leaves connection failures and silent stalls consuming capacity unnecessarily.

Timeout handling must propagate cancellation to upstream requests, retry loops, and associated work rather than merely stop waiting downstream. Connection-pool cleanup must release accounting and discard connections with unread or protocol-ambiguous data; multiplexed protocols may permit cancelling only the affected stream. After a partial streaming response reaches the client, the gateway generally cannot substitute a clean error response or retry transparently, so it must terminate the stream and record the failure.

## Operational guidance

Choose limits by endpoint behavior and service objectives, define precisely when each clock starts and resets, and monitor expirations separately. Include queueing and retries in the overall budget, and test cancellation and cleanup under load.

Operational rule: enforce every applicable deadline, propagate the earliest expiry, and verify resources are reclaimed.
